title: Reading the Psalms and the Gospels in Latin

objectives.can: Read a Psalm and a Gospel chapter in the Vulgate with reduced help.

explanation.summary: Psalm 22 and the Gospel of John show the two voices of the Latin Bible: the Psalms are short, parallel, personal lines that often leave a word out; the Gospels tell a story in a run of short clauses. This lesson gives you a method for each, and then you read the Psalm with only the Latin to lean on.

sections.heading: Finding the Psalm: numbering and titles
body: The Vulgate numbers the Psalms as the Greek Old Testament does, so for most of the Psalter its number is one less than the number in a Hebrew-based Bible. The shepherd Psalm that is Psalm 23 in many English Bibles is Psalm 22 here. The library's chapter references follow the Latin, and so does this lesson.

In Latin the title is part of verse 1: *Psalmus David* stands before *Dominus regit me*. The Douay English beside each verse is translated from the Latin, which is why it says 'The Lord ruleth me', following *regit*.

sections.heading: How a Psalm is built
body: A Psalm is poetry, but not poetry of rhyme or metre. Its main device is parallelism: two lines say the same thing, or build on each other. In verse 4, *Virga tua, et baculus tuus* names two things that comfort; in verse 5, *Parasti ... impinguasti* is a pair of verbs, both addressed to God. Read the lines together and let the second one add to the first.

A Psalm often leaves things out. A verb may be missing: in Psalm 26:1 *Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea* has no verb, and you supply *est*, 'is'. A subject may be missing: in Psalm 22:2–3 the verbs *collocavit*, *educavit*, *convertit* and *deduxit* have no stated subject, and the subject is the *Dominus* of verse 1, carried forward. Latin does not need a pronoun to show the subject, because the verb ending shows person and number.

A Psalm also changes its address. Verses 1 to 3 speak about the Lord in the third person; from *quoniam tu mecum es* in verse 4 the speaker turns and speaks to him, in the second person (*tu*, *Parasti*, *impinguasti*). The change does not need a mark: it shows in the person endings.

sections.heading: Some Latin details of this Psalm
body: *nihil mihi deerit* uses the dative *mihi* with *desum*: 'nothing will be lacking to me'. The subject is *nihil*, and *mihi* shows for whom.

*etsi ambulavero* in verse 4 has a future perfect after *etsi*: 'even if I shall have walked' in the sense of 'even if I walk'. The verb looks ahead to a time when the walking is done. *quoniam tu mecum es* then gives the ground of the trust: 'because you are with me'.

*ipsa me consolata sunt* has a passive-looking form but an active sense: *consolor* is a deponent verb (a verb passive in form, active in meaning). The neuter plural *ipsa* sums up the two things, rod and staff, so the verb is plural. *propter nomen suum* in verse 3 uses the reflexive *suum*: 'for his own name', referring to the subject of the sentence, the Lord.

sections.heading: Reading a Gospel chapter
body: Gospel narrative is plainer. It runs in short clauses, usually joined by *et*, with verbs in the perfect or imperfect and speech reported directly. John 1:29 is typical: *vidit Joannes Jesum venientem ad se, et ait: Ecce agnus Dei*. *vidit* is a perfect, *venientem* a participle agreeing with *Jesum* and describing him as he came ('saw Jesus coming'), and *ait* introduces the speech.

The prologue of John is the nearest the Gospels come to the Psalms in form. John 1:4, *In ipso vita erat, et vita erat lux hominum*, repeats *vita* to link two lines, much as a Psalm links its parallel lines. Notice *erat* again and again: John uses the imperfect of 'to be' to say what already was, and the repeated word is the stitching of the passage.

Dialogue is introduced by verbs such as *ait*, *dixit* and *respondit*. After *ecce*, expect a noun or a relative clause: *ecce agnus Dei, ecce qui tollit peccatum mundi*, 'behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sin of the world'.

sections.heading: A method for reduced help
body: Read each verse aloud first, finding the verb or verbs. Say who or what the subject is, and whether it is stated. Notice what is left out and supply it. Only then look at the English, and use it to check, not to find out. A good test: cover the English, read the Latin, say the sense in your own words, and uncover to see how close you were.

misunderstandings: Confusing the Vulgate's Psalm numbers with the numbers in an English Bible. They usually differ by one.
Reading the two lines of a parallel pair as two separate events. The second line normally repeats, extends or sharpens the first.
Treating the perfect in a Psalm only as 'did'. *Parasti* and *impinguasti* are perfects that the English renders 'hast prepared' and 'hast anointed'; the Latin perfect covers both.
Seeing a missing verb as an error. In poetry a form of 'to be' is often understood, as in *Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea*.

deeper.heading: Which Latin Psalter?
body: The Psalms printed in the Vulgate used here are generally taken to be Jerome's revision of an older Latin Psalter against the Greek, and not a fresh translation from the Hebrew. That is one reason the numbering follows the Greek. Readers who want the Hebrew-based text should look for the separate version of the Psalms that Jerome made from Hebrew, which this library does not hold.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: A psalm for David. The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *Dominus* is the subject of *regit*, and the pronoun object *me* shows who is ruled. *nihil mihi deerit*: *deerit* is a future of *desum*, with *mihi* in the dative. The two clauses are parallel: the Lord rules, and for that reason nothing will be lacking.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: He hath converted my soul. He hath led me on the paths of justice, for his own name’s sake.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *animam meam convertit* and *Deduxit me super semitas* are two parallel lines with the same subject, the Lord, left unstated. *convertit* and *Deduxit* are both past (perfect) forms of the verbs *converto* and *deduco*. The line ends with *propter nomen suum*; *suum* is the reflexive possessive and refers back to the subject, the Lord.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me. Thy rod and thy staff, they have comforted me.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *etsi ambulavero* is 'even if I walk', with a future perfect. *non timebo mala* is the main clause: 'I will not fear evils'. *quoniam tu mecum es* gives the reason and turns the Psalm to address God directly. The last clause, *Virga tua, et baculus tuus, ipsa me consolata sunt*, has a deponent *consolata sunt*, active in sense.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: The psalm of David before he was anointed. The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea*: three nouns in the nominative with no verb. The verb 'is' is understood, as Hebrew poetry often leaves it out. *illuminatio* and *salus* are both predicate nouns, linked by *et*.

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: The next day, John saw Jesus coming to him, and he saith: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *vidit Joannes Jesum venientem*: *vidit* is a perfect, the accusative *Jesum* is its object, and *venientem* is a present participle agreeing with it. *ait* introduces what John said, and *ecce* points: 'behold'. *ecce qui tollit peccatum mundi*: the relative *qui* with the verb *tollit* describes the one pointed to.
